analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable patient rights in managed care plans and expands tax breaks for health coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 106th Congress with three Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a set of patient rights into the laws governing employer health plans and insurers: coverage of emergency care without prior approval, direct access to obstetricians and pediatricians, timely access to specialists, continued treatment when a doctor leaves the network, independent outside appeals of claim denials, and limited new rights to sue when a plan's denial is not a medical judgment. It would also expand tax-favored medical savings accounts, let self-employed people deduct all of their health insurance costs, and push health plans toward a single standard claim form. It was introduced on November 3, 2000, nine weeks before the Congress ended, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in employer-sponsored and managed care health plans gain the most: the bill requires plans to cover emergency services and emergency ambulance transport on the plan's in-network terms without prior authorization, lets women see an OB/GYN without a referral, lets parents designate a pediatrician, guarantees coverage of an out-of-network specialist when no in-network specialist is available, lets patients finish an active course of treatment for up to 90 days (through pregnancy and, for terminal illness, for life) after their doctor is dropped from the network, bars plans from gagging doctors from discussing treatment options, requires coverage of routine costs for patients in approved cancer clinical trials, and creates internal and independent external appeals with strict deadlines, including 72-hour expedited decisions [S3]. Patients also gain the right to sue in court over certain plan denials under the remedies title [S2]. Separately, self-employed individuals could deduct 100 percent of health insurance costs, and medical savings accounts would be opened beyond small employers and the self-employed with larger deductions [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency department services and emergency ambulance transport with no prior authorization, and the patient cannot be charged more than if an in-network provider had treated them, using a 'prudent layperson' standard for what counts as an emergency [S3].
Women get direct access to obstetric and gynecological care without a referral, and parents may designate a pediatrician as their child's primary care provider [S3].

Patients undergoing active treatment for a serious or complex condition, hospitalization, pregnancy, or terminal illness may continue with their doctor for a transitional period — up to 90 days, through postpartum care, or for life in terminal illness — after the plan drops the provider from its network [S3].

Plans must set claim-determination deadlines (72 hours for expedited prior-authorization decisions), bar compensation arrangements that reward reviewers for denying claims, and provide internal appeals plus independent external appeals of denials [S3].

The remedies title amends ERISA to make court remedies available for medically reviewable coverage determinations and expands remedies for non-medically-reviewable determinations, giving patients recourse beyond lost benefits [S2].
Plans may not deny cancer patients participation in approved clinical trials or withhold coverage of routine patient care costs connected to the trial [S3].

Self-employed individuals get a deduction for 100 percent of their health insurance costs, and medical savings accounts become available to workers beyond small employers with bigger allowable deductions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and insurers bear the compliance costs: new coverage mandates, utilization-review and appeals machinery, disclosure requirements, and the administrative cost of external review, plus exposure to limited new lawsuits over claim denials [S2, S3]. Employers sponsoring group plans face disclosure duties (including annually reporting what they contribute to each employee's coverage) and the risk that mandated protections raise premiums, which ultimately flow into wages or premiums paid by workers [S3]. The tax provisions reduce federal revenue through larger health-related deductions [S2].

drawbacks.text: The tax title expands medical savings accounts and lets self-employed people deduct all health insurance costs — deductions worth the most to those with high incomes and high tax bills, and a design whose effect on conventional insurance costs the bill itself directs the Comptroller General to study before judging [S2].

The point-of-service choice requirement does not apply to employers with fewer than 25 employees if compliance would raise their overall costs, and plans may pass the added cost of out-of-network options on to the employees who choose them [S3].

The bill would let insurers offer high-deductible plans exempt from paying for items and services subject to the deductible, and would preempt state payment laws for those plans after five years unless states reenact them — weakening state patient protections [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that mandated benefits and appeals processes raise plan costs, and that some employers respond to higher premiums by dropping coverage or shifting more cost to workers.

The remedies title both expands and limits court remedies, so a patient denied a medically reviewable benefit would still face narrower recourse than full malpractice-style liability would provide [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients in managed care, the protections address real, documented failure modes — blocked emergency care, no direct OB-GYN access, denials with no outside review — and the appeals and disclosure rules are the kind of regulation whose costs are modest relative to the harm prevented. The main design weakness is the tax title: expanding medical savings accounts and full self-employed deductions mainly reduces taxes for people who already buy coverage or can afford high deductibles, and the bill itself concedes uncertainty by ordering a study of the effect on conventional insurance costs. The carve-outs for small employers and the preemption of some state laws trim the protections. On balance the consumer protections are the substance of the bill; the tax incentives are a rider that mainly helps higher-income households.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with nine weeks left in the 106th Congress, the bill was referred to three House committees and their health subcommittees, where nothing happened, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative John Shadegg introduced the bill on November 3, 2000, joined by Representatives Coburn, Salmon, and Aderholt; all four were Republicans [S1, S3].

The Speaker referred it to the Committees on Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means, splitting its patient-rights, tax, and employer provisions across panels with separate jurisdictions [S5].
Within a week it was sent to the Health subcommittee of Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history; the last recorded action is the subcommittee referral of November 8, 2000, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans and insurers are better off: the new coverage mandates, appeals deadlines, disclosure duties, and limited lawsuit exposure never took effect. Patients in managed care plans are in the same position as before the bill was written.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, but no committee action, vote, or recorded opposition exists, so no partisan split on the bill's merits can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill imposes coverage mandates, external appeals, utilization-review rules, disclosure duties, and limited new lawsuit exposure on plans — costs their interest runs against. But it also expands the tax-favored medical savings account market they could sell into and preempts some state payment laws for high-deductible plans, so its effects on the industry pull in both directions [S2, S3].

Employers face new disclosure duties, including annually reporting what they contribute to each employee's coverage, and bear premium increases if mandated protections raise costs — though the smallest employers (under 25 workers) are exempt from the point-of-service requirement [S3].

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: The bill bars plans from gagging doctors' medical advice, requires prompt payment of clean claims, bans incentive arrangements that reward claim denials, mandates independent external appeals, and guarantees transitional payment when a doctor is dropped mid-treatment — easing the pressure managed care puts on providers [S3].
